rules.statement: Don't report a trailing `CancellationToken` parameter on one of our own async methods as unused or misleading just because none of its awaited calls takes a token today, and don't suggest dropping it or suppressing the cancellation-token analyzer rule.
rules.why: Every async method of ours takes a `CancellationToken` even when no callee accepts one. The token is part of the method's contract, so a call added later honors it. Only a method an ADR explicitly makes uncancellable, whose work runs on its own token, takes none.
rules.check: Before reporting an unused token, check whether the method is ours and async, and whether any ADR declares it uncancellable. If the callees just take no token, don't raise a finding. This applies to production and test helpers alike.

rules.statement: Don't suggest adding `cancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` to an async method only so that a token its callees can't take is used.
rules.why: It turns token-less work into a cancellation point, which changes the method's behavior.
rules.check: Look for findings or fixes that add `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` purely to consume an otherwise unobserved token. Don't propose them.

rules.statement: Don't ask for default values on parameters that come before a trailing `CancellationToken`, and don't report call sites that pass each of those arguments explicitly, including `null`.
rules.why: No optional parameter may come before the token, so every caller must pass each input explicitly.
rules.check: When a finding complains about positional `null` arguments or lost defaults ahead of a trailing `CancellationToken`, confirm the token is the required last parameter. If it is, don't raise the finding.

rules.statement: Give every parameter of a documented method a `<param>` tag, including a `CancellationToken`. When the token isn't observed, the tag must say so and why, not claim it is monitored for cancellation.
rules.why: IntelliSense otherwise gives no description of the parameter, and a doc that says the token is monitored leads callers to expect cancellation that never happens.
rules.check: Find methods with `///` docs that gained a parameter without a `<param>`, and `<param name="cancellationToken">` text that says 'monitor for cancellation' on a token the body never reads.

rules.statement: When a declaration moves or a new declaration is inserted, keep each `//` comment directly above the code it describes.
rules.why: A comment left above the wrong declaration describes the wrong code.
rules.check: Look in the diff for a new member inserted between an existing comment and the member that comment describes.

rules.statement: In a Roslyn analyzer test project, pin each exemption boundary with tests on both sides, including symbols declared in a referenced assembly and explicit interface implementations, and add a test that generated code (`// <auto-generated/>`) reports nothing.
rules.why: A regression in an exemption check or in the generated-code flag could otherwise silently exempt the code's own members, flag contract implementations, or break builds of Razor and source-generator output, with no test failing.
rules.check: For an analyzer change that adds or changes an exemption or `ConfigureGeneratedCodeAnalysis`, look for tests covering both the reported case and the exempt case, a referenced-assembly case, explicit interface implementations, and generated code.

rules.statement: In a Roslyn analyzer, don't filter methods to `MethodKind.Ordinary` alone when the rule should also cover explicit interface implementations. Also accept `MethodKind.ExplicitInterfaceImplementation` and let the exemption logic decide.
rules.why: An early return on `MethodKind.Ordinary` silently skips explicit implementations, so they escape the diagnostic and the exemption check for them never runs.
rules.check: Look for `method.MethodKind != MethodKind.Ordinary` early returns in analyzers whose exemption logic handles interface implementations.
